name: Acetyl carnitine

lead: Acetyl-L-carnitine (ALCAR) is made naturally in the body and sold as an oral supplement. Carnitine helps move fatty acids into mitochondria for energy, and the acetyl form is also studied for nerve and brain function.

Its appearance link is indirect: people in physique and training communities take it hoping for better fat use, energy and recovery, which could support training and body composition. No trial has tested it for appearance outcomes.

paras: It is taken orally as capsules or powder, often alongside other training supplements. Forum members discuss it in the context of post-workout stacks and energy.
Reviews describe few adverse effects. Studies in chemotherapy-induced neuropathy gave mixed results, with one trial suggesting it may have worsened neuropathy under taxane therapy.

chain: Supplies carnitine for fatty acid transport
May support training and leaner physique (claimed)
angle.text: People take it hoping to support fat metabolism and training energy. The link to appearance is through training and body composition, and is not directly tested.

lead: Acetyl-L-carnitine (also levacecarnine) is an acetylated form of L-carnitine that the body makes naturally and that is sold as an over-the-counter oral supplement. Enzymes convert it to carnitine, which helps carry fatty acids into mitochondria for energy [1][2].

In physique-oriented communities it is discussed among supplements for energy and recovery. The chain to looks is indirect: better energy use and recovery could support training volume and body composition. A small human study linked intravenous ALCAR to greater fat use and less glucose use [1].
Research covers neuropathy, male infertility, dementia, depression and others, with mixed results [1][3][4].

paras: Humans make carnitine from lysine in a multistep pathway that needs vitamin C, iron, vitamin B6 and NAD+, and also take it in from food, mainly animal products such as red meat.[5] Wikipedia reports that omnivores take in roughly 23 to 135 mg a day and vegans about 10 to 12 mg, and that deficiency in healthy people is rare.[5] Free carnitine ferries long-chain fatty acids into mitochondria, and carnitine acetyltransferase moves excess acetyl groups out of them; acetyl-carnitine is the acetylated ester that carries those groups.[2][5] A 1964 Nature paper described acetyl-carnitine in heart and liver tissue.[6] A 1985 review noted that the acetyl-carnitine to carnitine ratio in tissue changes with nutritional state and helps regulate coenzyme A synthesis.[7]

Wikipedia gives 1905 as the year carnitine was first extracted from meat extract and 27 December 1985 as the date the US FDA approved levocarnitine as the prescription product Carnitor.[5] Acetyl-L-carnitine itself is sold as an over-the-counter dietary supplement in capsule and powder form.
Supplement uses include energy support and cognitive claims. A 1989 study examined chronic and acute effects of L-carnitine in elite athletes [8].

Athletes use carnitine products to support energy use and recovery. Wikipedia's carnitine article describes the research on athletes as low in quality: at multi-gram daily amounts over a month, no consistent benefit appeared for moderate-intensity exercise and results for high-intensity exercise were mixed. A 2021 systematic review it cites was described as inconclusive, and it states that supplements do not appear to raise muscle carnitine levels.[5] That article also reports no evidence that L-carnitine changes fat metabolism or aids weight loss; these findings concern L-carnitine rather than the acetyl form specifically.[5]

Neuropathy meta-analyses (2015, 2017) suggested reduced pain while a 2019 Cochrane review was uncertain; a 2003 Cochrane review found little evidence in Alzheimer's disease; a 2018 meta-analysis of 12 trials found depression symptom reduction versus placebo [1]. A meta-analysis examined L-carnitine/acetyl-carnitine or N-acetylcysteine in men with idiopathic asthenozoospermia [9]. An older crossover trial studied it in depressed elderly subjects [10].
Reviews report few adverse effects [1]. One trial found it did not prevent chemotherapy neuropathy and may have worsened it with taxanes [1].

For carnitine more broadly, Wikipedia lists nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, diarrhea and a fish-like body odor at around 3 g a day, and notes that the antiepileptic drugs valproic acid, phenobarbital, phenytoin and carbamazepine can lower blood carnitine.[5] People who take medication are generally advised to check with a clinician before starting supplements.
Carnitine is central to moving fatty acids into mitochondria [1][7]. ALCAR may donate acetyl groups, increasing mGluR2 expression [1].
T Nation forum members mention it in post-workout and energy supplement discussions [11][12].

On T Nation, a 2001 post-workout thread lists acetyl carnitine alongside HMB and TMG as products a member was considering adding to a BCAA and taurine formula.[11] A 2014 thread on staying alert at work names acetyl-L-carnitine with N-acetyl-tyrosine and a B complex as nootropics a poster suggested for tiredness.[13] A 2017 long-running thread includes a reply that acetyl-L-carnitine, vitamin D and B and C vitamins show some promise for long COVID symptoms, with the reply noting there is no great research on that.[14]
A 2023 competition log from an amateur classic physique competitor shows the kind of detailed diet and supplement tracking in which such products appear.[12]

Beyond appearance, ALCAR is studied for mitochondrial support in neurological disease: a 2024 review of mitochondria in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis lists acetyl-carnitine among mitochondria-directed strategies examined in preclinical and clinical work.[15] A 2021 meta-analysis of seven trials with 621 men with idiopathic asthenozoospermia found that L-carnitine/L-acetyl-carnitine improved sperm motility and normal morphology compared with placebo, without a significant change in concentration.[9]
Human studies address neuropathy, infertility, depression and dementia [1][9][10][3]. No studies found for skin, hair or physique appearance outcomes.

lore.intro: Acetyl-L-carnitine appears in training forums mostly as an add-on in post-workout, energy and nootropic stacks rather than as a headline product.[11][13]
